title: KV cache eviction & prefix reuse deep dive with Ventra Systems
summary: Deep technical troubleshooting session on KV cache eviction patterns observed in Ventra's long-context chat workload. Reviewed eviction triggers, paging behavior, prefix reuse implications, and suggestions for benchmarking and config tuning. Agreed next steps to run targeted load tests and share logs and heap profiles.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-15
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 65 minutes
Attendees: Mia Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Redwood PM), Liam O'Rourke (Ventra CTO), Ayesha Malik (Ventra Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Ventra Infra)

[00:00] Mia Chen: Morning everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll hand off to Carlos for the deep dive on the KV cache behavior you've been seeing.
[00:10] Liam O'Rourke: Yep thanks Mia. We really want to understand why we're getting these cache evictions mid-session, it breaks continuity for our agents.
[00:20] Carlos Ortega: Cool. So I'll share my screen in a sec. Just to set expectations, this call will go through the observed patterns, suspected root causes - eviction thresholds, paging, prefix reuse - and then propose tests.
[00:35] Ayesha Malik: one note, the logs we uploaded are from our dedicated cluster on-prem, we're on 8xA100, quantized to int8 for inference, and using the latest redwood runtime. there may be infra limits too.
[00:50] Carlos Ortega: Okay good, that helps. quick correction - sometimes the artifacts call it "Redwood Dedicate" in the telemetry, small typos in the exporter, so ignore that.
[01:05] Priya Raman: also, our PM asked about business impact thresholds - what's an acceptable drop in continuity vs cost. we'll cover that in the end.
[01:20] Carlos Ortega: jumping into the data - first pattern: evictions concentrated when sequence window grows above ~12k tokens. We see the KV cache memory footprint rising and then a hard eviction sweep.
[01:40] Samir Patel: to be clear, our requests are often multi-turn with long system prompts + user history, sometimes 20k-30k tokens depending on conversation.
[01:50] Carlos Ortega: right, and that matches. The runtime uses an LRU-ish policy with size buckets; when KV memory crosses the per-device threshold it starts evicting older KV pages. We also observed backpressure that increases per-token latency prior to eviction.
[02:10] Ayesha Malik: can you explain the difference between paging vs eviction in your runtime? our ops folks assume paging means using host memory but we want exact behavior.
[02:25] Carlos Ortega: good question. In our runtime, paging is an intermediate step - rare in hosted but possible on-private - where cold KV pages are migrated out of GPU to host pinned memory (if configured) before being dropped. Eviction is the runtime dropping KV pages entirely to free GPU memory. Paging adds latency when pages are brought back in. Eviction causes correctness issues if that KV data is required later unless there's prefix reuse handling.
[02:55] Liam O'Rourke: we saw both - a latency spike and then a context "forget" mid-chat. so perhaps paging was attempted but ultimately evicted?
[03:10] Carlos Ortega: yeah, the traces show migrate attempts around 11-13k token region, followed by eviction sweeps. Looks like the host pinned memory pool was configured but the allocator fell back due to fragmentation.
[03:25] Ayesha Malik: fragmentation how? like CUDA pinned memory fragmentation?
[03:33] Carlos Ortega: exactly - on-prem host pinned allocator can fragment, especially if other processes are allocating pinned buffers. We saw OOM logs for the pinned pool in the morning trace.
[03:45] Samir Patel: we do have monitoring for cudaMalloc failures but the exporter didn't surface pinned pool OOM specifically - we'll adjust.
[03:55] Carlos Ortega: second pattern - prefix reuse. When your application reuses prefixes (e.g., repeated system prompt templates across sessions) we expect reuse to reduce KV footprint if prefix reuse hashing is aligned. But if your prompt includes ephemeral tokens like timestamps or request IDs, the hashes differ and the runtime can't reuse pages, causing duplicate KV entries.
[04:25] Ayesha Malik: oh wow we do inject request ids into the system prompt for tracing. that could be the culprit.
[04:33] Mia Chen: that's a very common gotcha. If the prefix contains any variable token, reuse breaks. Carlos, do we have tooling to detect near-duplicate prefixes?
[04:45] Carlos Ortega: yes we've got a prefix reuse heatmap in the KV dashboard. I pulled a snippet - you can see high cardinality in the prefix keys for Ventra between 09:00-11:00 in the traces. I'll share the link after.
[05:00] Priya Raman: what's the immediate mitigation if we can't remove the request id? can we canonicalize or strip it before sending to the model?
[05:10] Carlos Ortega: strip is best. Alternatively you can place mutable metadata in a tool call or a separate metadata header that doesn't participate in the prompt body. For short term, we can enable prefix hashing with a normalization hook on the SE side.
[05:25] Ayesha Malik: interesting. what about the eviction thresholds - can we tune them?
[05:30] Carlos Ortega: yes. On Dedicated/Private you can raise the KV budget per-device, adjust the eviction aggressiveness, and configure a larger pinned memory pool for paging. There is cost and latency trade-off - increasing GPU reserved memory reduces capacity for batching.
[05:45] Samir Patel: that bump would reduce our instance density which we want to avoid. do you have recommendations for trade-offs?
[05:55] Carlos Ortega: we usually recommend a multi-pronged approach: 1) prefix normalization to reduce duplication, 2) gentle increase in pinned pool and KV budget, 3) enable smarter batching to compact repeated prefixes in the same batch, which increases reuse, 4) tune quantization profile to slightly reduce KV size if model supports it.
[06:20] Ayesha Malik: quantization affects KV size? I thought it changes compute.
[06:25] Carlos Ortega: it does both. Lower-precision keys and values use less memory in KV. Int8 or 4-bit quant can reduce KV footprint significantly, but you must validate quality - especially for long-context attention. There can be numerical drift affecting retrieval.
[06:45] Liam O'Rourke: can you give a rough number - how much KV reduction with int8 vs fp16?
[06:50] Carlos Ortega: depends on implementation; ballpark int8 can be ~2x smaller than fp16 for stored KV. But quantized kernels may also change latency characteristics. We saw some customers choose int8 for throughput and accept small affinity changes.
[07:10] Priya Raman: on the topic of batching you mentioned - our traffic is heavy tail per user, many smaller sessions. Is batching still beneficial?
[07:20] Carlos Ortega: yes, batching by similar prefix shapes increases the chance that KV pages are reused in the same batch and not duplicated across microbatches. There's also continuous batching heuristics in the runtime that try to match similar context lengths. But high prefix cardinality reduces this benefit.
[07:40] Ayesha Malik: ok. let's get practical - what's the recommended test plan we should run to isolate the issue?
[07:50] Carlos Ortega: propose three tests: 1) Synthetic long-context run with canonicalized prefixes (no request ids) to measure baseline KV growth and eviction threshold. 2) same load with request ids injected to measure duplication. 3) run with increased pinned pool and kv_budget to see if paging prevents eviction and observe latency impact. We'll provide a harness and a script to replay your traces.
[08:15] Mia Chen: note we'll provide our replay harness and a sample workload template. We'll also share the KV dashboard link and the specific trace IDs.
[08:25] Ayesha Malik: thanks. on the traces you mentioned fragmentation - is there a way Redwood can defensively avoid pinned OOM by proactively failing earlier or fall back to a conservative policy?
[08:40] Carlos Ortega: runtime does have a fallback - if paging fails it will attempt aggressive eviction. we can add a soft limit warning earlier but that requires exporter changes. For now we can set a lower paging threshold so it evicts earlier rather than attempt expensive host migration.
[09:00] Samir Patel: how about visibility - what logs should we capture to send you?
[09:05] Carlos Ortega: attach KV memstats, eviction events, pinned pool alloc/fail, per-token latency traces, and the per-request prefix hash. If possible, collect a short perf trace (20-30s) during a high-watermark session. We'll include the log parsers.
[09:25] Ayesha Malik: we'll capture those.
[09:28] Carlos Ortega: quick aside - we also saw repeated small evictions at ~6-7k tokens in one trace. That suggested prefix reuse was partially working but fragmentation prevented efficient reuse.
[09:45] Liam O'Rourke: so it's not just size threshold, it's fragmentation + high-cardinality prefixes + pinned pool OOMs.
[09:55] Carlos Ortega: correct. Another observation - when eviction occurs mid-response, the model can continue but will lose earlier KV entries, which looks like the generation forgetting context. That is especially visible when you have repeated named entities.
[10:15] Ayesha Malik: any quick patch we can do at the model prompt layer to reduce severity?
[10:20] Carlos Ortega: yes - compress older conversation turns into summaries and keep only the distilled tokens in the prompt. That reduces KV growth. We can also create per-session short-term caches for active tokens and flush older ones intentionally.
[10:35] Priya Raman: question about correctness - if we summarize older tokens, are we changing model outputs significantly?
[10:40] Carlos Ortega: depends on your use case. Many customers accept condensed history because it preserves intent while reducing token count. But it's a business decision. We can help run A/B evals.
[10:55] Mia Chen: let's pivot to backlog - any infra changes recommended for on-prem? Samir?
[11:00] Carlos Ortega: for on-prem, increase host pinned mem pool, ensure eviction logs are shipped, and try to isolate other pinned allocators. Also consider node pinning: dedicate inference nodes to avoid host fragmentation.
[11:15] Samir Patel: we can dedicate nodes, though that reduces flexibility. is there a way to set per-tenant quotas?
[11:24] Carlos Ortega: yes, Dedicated and Private modes support per-tenant KV budgets and per-route limits. We can set a soft quota for Ventra sessions.
[11:32] Ayesha Malik: earlier you said duplicate KV pages from prefixes increase memory - can we dedupe at the exporter before sending payload to the runtime?
[11:40] Carlos Ortega: good thought - if you canonicalize the prompt at the SDK layer and strip variable tokens before sending, that avoids duplicates. We'll attach a sample canonicalization function.
[11:50] Mia Chen: I'm going to note action: Carlos share canonicalization snippet and dashboard links.
[11:56] Carlos Ortega: noted. I'll also share a short runbook: when you see mid-session forget, check eviction events, examine prefix cardinality, inspect pinned pool OOMs.
[12:10] Ayesha Malik: we saw a specific session id where the model forgot a user's name after a long turn. we'll send that session id.
[12:18] Carlos Ortega: please do, that'll help us root cause faster.
[12:23] Liam O'Rourke: one concern - if we increase KV budgets, will you bill us differently for Dedicated?
[12:30] Mia Chen: yes there are capacity impacts, we'll include cost estimates in the POC template. We'll show delta per-device and suggested commit for Dedicated.
[12:40] Priya Raman: can you also run a simulated cost/latency curve for kv_budget increments? like +10%, +25% and show throughput impact?
[12:50] Carlos Ortega: we can, we'll run microbenchmarks with your model and quant profile. For now, expected trade-off: more KV reserved memory reduces batch concurrency so throughput per-GPU falls. But tail latency and continuity improves.
[13:05] Samir Patel: any notes on KMS or encryption when paging to host memory? is data encrypted in pinned memory?
[13:12] Carlos Ortega: pinned memory is not encrypted by CUDA; if you need encryption at rest for KV pages when paging, we currently recommend avoiding paging to host in regulated workloads or enabling host-level memory encryption and secure enclaves. For Private we can route pages to an encrypted host storage if necessary but that's heavier.
[13:35] Ayesha Malik: that pushes us to prefer eviction over paging for compliance, though eviction breaks continuity. tough tradeoff.
[13:45] Carlos Ortega: that's why prefix normalization is the low-friction fix.
[13:52] Mia Chen: ok let's summarize next steps and owners.
[14:00] Carlos Ortega: Summary recap: root causes likely high prefix cardinality + pinned pool fragmentation causing paging attempts and then eviction. Recommended fixes: prefix canonicalization, increased pinned pool or lower paging threshold, kv_budget bump, quantization validation, batching by prefix similarity. Tests: run 3 synthetic tests (canonicalized, with request ids, with increased kv_budget) and provide traces.
[14:28] Ayesha Malik: thanks that's clear. we'll run tests and send traces and host metrics.
[14:34] Mia Chen: final question from Ventra - can Redwood run the POC on a short term Dedicated pool under our account to run benchmarks?
[14:42] Mia Chen: we can spin up a short trial Dedicated cluster for this POC, we'll include costs and duration in the follow up email.
[14:50] Liam O'Rourke: great. scheduling - propose follow-up next Thu same time?
[14:56] Mia Chen: sounds good. we'll send calendar invite.
[15:00] Carlos Ortega: ok I'll collect the dashboard links and scripts and upload them to the shared drive. Expect an email with steps and a replay harness.
[15:10] Ayesha Malik: thanks everyone.
[15:12] Mia Chen: thanks, meeting adjourned.
